ph-t15.subject: Physics
ph-t15.question: I'm a Physics SL student (the course first assessed in 2025; my exams are in May 2027). Paper 2 practice question. A railway wagon of mass 1.2 × 10⁴ kg is released from rest at the top of a slope and rolls down through a vertical height of 0.46 m. Ignore friction and air resistance. (a) Show that the speed of the wagon at the bottom of the slope is about 3.0 m s⁻¹. [2] On the level track the wagon, moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹, collides with a stationary wagon of mass 8.0 × 10³ kg, and the two wagons couple together. (b) Calculate the speed of the coupled wagons just after the collision. [2] (c) Calculate the kinetic energy transferred to other forms in the collision, and express it as a percentage of the kinetic energy before the collision. [3] (d) The coupled wagons are brought to rest by a buffer in 0.60 s. Calculate the average force exerted by the buffer on the wagons. [2] (e) The buffer contains a spring of spring constant 2.0 × 10⁶ N m⁻¹. Assuming that all the kinetic energy of the coupled wagons is stored in the spring, calculate its maximum compression in cm. [2] (f) Explain why the total momentum of the wagons is conserved in the collision but their kinetic energy is not. [2] Show your working with units.
ph-t15.response_text:
Assumptions: g = 9.8 m s⁻² (the data booklet value, since the question gives no value for g); friction and air resistance are ignored; the 3.0 m s⁻¹ in (b) is the value given in the question.

(a) [2]
Principle: with no friction, the gravitational potential energy lost equals the kinetic energy gained, and the wagon starts from rest.
mgh = ½mv²
The mass cancels: v² = 2gh
Substitution: v² = 2 × 9.8 m s⁻² × 0.46 m = 9.016 m² s⁻²
v = √9.016 m² s⁻² = 3.0027 m s⁻², so v = 3.00 m s⁻¹ (3 s.f.)
This agrees with the value given, 3.0 m s⁻¹.

(b) [2]
Principle: momentum is conserved, since no external horizontal force acts during the collision.
m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v
(1.2 × 10⁴ kg)(3.0 m s⁻¹) + (8.0 × 10³ kg)(0) = (1.2 × 10⁴ kg + 8.0 × 10³ kg)v
3.6 × 10⁴ kg m s⁻¹ = (2.0 × 10⁴ kg)v
v = 1.8 m s⁻¹, in the original direction of motion

(c) [3]
Before: E_k = ½m₁u₁² = ½(1.2 × 10⁴ kg)(3.0 m s⁻¹)² = 5.4 × 10⁴ J
After: E_k = ½(m₁ + m₂)v² = ½(2.0 × 10⁴ kg)(1.8 m s⁻¹)² = 3.24 × 10⁴ J
Transferred to other forms: ΔE = 5.4 × 10⁴ J − 3.24 × 10⁴ J = 2.16 × 10⁴ J, so ΔE = 2.2 × 10⁴ J (2 s.f.)
As a percentage: (2.16 × 10⁴ J / 5.4 × 10⁴ J) × 100% = 40%

(d) [2]
Principle: impulse equals change in momentum, FΔt = Δp.
Δp = m(v − u) = (2.0 × 10⁴ kg)(0 − 1.8 m s⁻¹) = −3.6 × 10⁴ kg m s⁻¹
F = Δp / Δt = (−3.6 × 10⁴ kg m s⁻¹) / (0.60 s) = −6.0 × 10⁴ N
The average force is 6.0 × 10⁴ N, opposite to the direction of motion.

(e) [2]
Principle: ½kx² = E_k, with E_k = 3.24 × 10⁴ J from (c).
x² = (2 × 3.24 × 10⁴ J) / (2.0 × 10⁶ N m⁻¹) = 3.24 × 10⁻² m²
x = 0.18 m = 18 cm (2 s.f.)

(f) [2]
Momentum: the forces between the wagons during coupling are an equal and opposite pair (Newton's third law), so they are internal to the system. The weights are balanced by normal forces and friction is ignored, so there is no external horizontal force and the total momentum is conserved.
Kinetic energy: the wagons stick together in an inelastic collision. Part of the kinetic energy becomes internal energy in the couplings (deformation and heating) and sound, so the kinetic energy after the collision is less, while the total energy is still conserved.

Next step: redo (b) with the 8.0 × 10³ kg wagon moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ towards the first wagon, and check the sign of your final velocity.

ch-t15.subject: Chemistry
ch-t15.question: I'm a Chemistry HL student (the course first assessed in 2025; my exams are in May 2027). Paper 2 practice question on the synthesis of ammonia: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). (a) Using the average bond enthalpies N≡N 945 kJ mol⁻¹, H–H 436 kJ mol⁻¹ and N–H 391 kJ mol⁻¹, calculate the enthalpy change of the forward reaction. [3] (b) The standard enthalpy change of this reaction is −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Suggest why your answer to (a) differs from this value. [1] (c) In a laboratory model, 600 cm³ of nitrogen and 1500 cm³ of hydrogen, measured at the same temperature and pressure, are mixed. Identify the limiting reactant and calculate the maximum volume of ammonia that could form at the same temperature and pressure. [3] (d) The mixture formed 150 cm³ of ammonia. Calculate the percentage yield. [1] (e) An equilibrium mixture in a sealed 2.00 dm³ vessel at 700 K contains 0.400 mol of N₂, 1.20 mol of H₂ and 0.200 mol of NH₃. Calculate the equilibrium constant, Kc, at 700 K. [3] (f) State and explain the effect of an increase in temperature on the value of Kc. [2] (g) Explain, in terms of the position of equilibrium and the rate of reaction, why the industrial process uses a high pressure and a moderate temperature. [3] Show your working with units.
ch-t15.response_text:
(a) Enthalpy change of the forward reaction [3]

N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)

Bonds broken: 1 × N≡N + 3 × H–H = 1 × 945 + 3 × 436 = 945 + 1308 = 2253 kJ [1]
Bonds formed: 6 × N–H (two NH₃ molecules, three N–H bonds each) = 6 × 391 = 2346 kJ [1]
ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed) = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

This value is for the reaction as written, which forms 2 mol of NH₃.

(b) Reason for the difference [1]

Average bond enthalpies are mean values taken over many compounds, and the calculation treats every species as a gas. The calculated value is therefore only an approximation of the true enthalpy change. [1]

(c) Limiting reactant and maximum volume of ammonia [3]

At the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules, so the volume ratio equals the mole ratio, N₂ : H₂ : NH₃ = 1 : 3 : 2.
Hydrogen needed for 600 cm³ of N₂ = 3 × 600 = 1800 cm³. Only 1500 cm³ of H₂ is available, so hydrogen is the limiting reactant. [1]
Check: nitrogen needed for 1500 cm³ of H₂ = 1500 ÷ 3 = 500 cm³. Since 600 cm³ is available, nitrogen is in excess.
Volume of NH₃ = 1500 cm³ H₂ × (2 ÷ 3) = 1000 cm³ [1]
Maximum volume of ammonia = 1.00 × 10³ cm³, at the same temperature and pressure. [1]

(d) Percentage yield [1]

percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100 = 150 cm³ ÷ 1000 cm³ × 100 = 15.0% [1]

(e) Equilibrium constant Kc at 700 K [3]

Concentration = amount ÷ volume, with V = 2.00 dm³:
[N₂] = 0.400 mol ÷ 2.00 dm³ = 0.200 mol dm⁻³
[H₂] = 1.20 mol ÷ 2.00 dm³ = 0.600 mol dm⁻³
[NH₃] = 0.200 mol ÷ 2.00 dm³ = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ [1]

Kc = [NH₃]² ÷ ([N₂][H₂]³) [1]
= (0.100)² ÷ (0.200 × 0.600³) = 0.0100 ÷ (0.200 × 0.216) = 0.0100 ÷ 0.0432 = 0.231 dm⁶ mol⁻² [1]

(f) Effect of an increase in temperature on Kc [2]

Kc decreases. [1]
The forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH is negative, as in part (a)). A rise in temperature shifts the position to the left, the endothermic direction, which absorbs the added heat. Fewer products and more reactants are present at equilibrium, so Kc falls. [1]

(g) Why high pressure and a moderate temperature are used [3]

High pressure: the position shifts to the right, the side with fewer gas molecules (2 mol of gas instead of 4 mol), which opposes the increase in pressure, so the equilibrium yield of ammonia increases. [1]
Higher pressure also increases the frequency of collisions between molecules, so the rate of reaction increases. [1]
Moderate temperature: a lower temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield, because the forward reaction is exothermic. However, fewer particles would then have energy at least equal to the activation energy, so the rate would be too slow. A moderate temperature gives a reasonable rate with an acceptable yield. [1]

bi-t15.subject: Biology
bi-t15.question: I'm a Biology SL student (the course first assessed in 2025; my exams are in May 2027). Paper 2 Section A data-based practice question. A 17-year-old student breathed into a spirometer at rest and again immediately after five minutes of step exercise (practice data written for this exercise). At rest: tidal volume 0.50 dm³ and 14 breaths per minute. After exercise: tidal volume 1.60 dm³ and 32 breaths per minute. From one deep breath at rest: inspiratory reserve volume 2.90 dm³ and expiratory reserve volume 1.20 dm³. (a) Calculate the ventilation rate (the volume of air breathed in per minute) at rest and after exercise. [2] (b) Calculate the percentage increase in the ventilation rate after exercise. [1] (c) Calculate the vital capacity of the student. [1] (d) Explain how the increase in ventilation after exercise helps to maintain the rate of gas exchange in the alveoli. [3] (e) Outline two adaptations of alveoli for gas exchange. [2] To make part (d) feel real, please also include the current number of people worldwide who have asthma and how many people died of asthma last year. Show your working.
bi-t15.response_text:
Assumptions: SL Biology, Paper 2 Section A, 9 marks across parts (a) to (e). The [1] tags are illustrative mark points for this practice question, not an official markscheme.

On the asthma figures: I cannot check current worldwide numbers in this session, so I have not included any. A current World Health Organization report, checked with your teacher, will give them, and the calculations below do not need them. Asthma narrows the airways, which limits the air reaching the alveoli, so it is a useful real-world link for part (d).

(a) Ventilation rate = tidal volume × breathing rate
At rest: 0.50 dm³ × 14 min⁻¹ = 7.0 dm³ min⁻¹ [1]
After exercise: 1.60 dm³ × 32 min⁻¹ = 51.2 dm³ min⁻¹ [1]

(b) Percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100
(51.2 − 7.0) ÷ 7.0 × 100 = 631.4%, so 631% to three significant figures; an increase of 631% [1]

(c) Vital capacity = inspiratory reserve volume + tidal volume + expiratory reserve volume
2.90 dm³ + 0.50 dm³ + 1.20 dm³ = 4.60 dm³ [1]

(d) Ventilation rises from 7.0 to 51.2 dm³ min⁻¹, about 7.3 times the resting rate, so far more air is moved in and out of the alveoli each minute. [1] This replaces the alveolar air, keeping the oxygen concentration in the alveoli high and the carbon dioxide concentration low, so the concentration gradients between alveolar air and blood stay steep. [1] Oxygen therefore diffuses into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses out, at a rate that meets the greater oxygen demand and carbon dioxide output of the respiring exercising muscles. [1] Blood flow through the alveolar capillaries also carries oxygen away and brings carbon dioxide in, which helps keep the gradients steep. [1 spare]

(e) Two adaptations of alveoli for gas exchange:
1. The alveolar wall is one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance. [1]
2. There are very many alveoli, giving a large total surface area for diffusion. [1]

ess-t15.subject: Environmental Systems and Societies
ess-t15.question: I'm an ESS SL student (the course first assessed in 2026; my exams are in May 2027). Paper 2 Section A data-based practice question. Students caught ground beetles in pitfall traps in two woodlands over one week in June (practice data written for this exercise). Woodland A, mixed broadleaf woodland: species 1, 12 individuals; species 2, 9; species 3, 7; species 4, 6; species 5, 4; species 6, 2. Woodland B, conifer plantation: species 1, 25 individuals; species 2, 8; species 3, 4; species 4, 2; species 5, 1. (a) Calculate Simpson's reciprocal index, D = N(N − 1) ÷ Σn(n − 1), for each woodland. [3] (b) Compare the biodiversity of the two woodlands, referring to species richness, evenness and your values of D. [3] (c) Suggest two reasons why the conifer plantation supports fewer ground-beetle species than the broadleaf woodland. [2] (d) Outline one limitation of using pitfall traps to compare the two woodlands. [1] (e) The plantation will be felled and left to regenerate naturally. Outline how its community could change over the next 50 years. [2] Show your working.
ess-t15.response_text:
(a) Simpson's reciprocal index has no unit for either woodland.

Method: N(N − 1) = 40 × 39 = 1560 for both woodlands, because N = 40 in each. [1]

Woodland A
N = 12 + 9 + 7 + 6 + 4 + 2 = 40
Σn(n − 1) = (12 × 11) + (9 × 8) + (7 × 6) + (6 × 5) + (4 × 3) + (2 × 1) = 132 + 72 + 42 + 30 + 12 + 2 = 290
D = 1560 ÷ 290 = 5.379…, so D = 5.38 (3 s.f.) [1]

Woodland B
N = 25 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 40
Σn(n − 1) = (25 × 24) + (8 × 7) + (4 × 3) + (2 × 1) + (1 × 0) = 600 + 56 + 12 + 2 + 0 = 670
D = 1560 ÷ 670 = 2.328…, so D = 2.33 (3 s.f.) [1]

(b) Woodland A has greater species richness than Woodland B, with 6 species against 5 [1].

Woodland A is also more even. Its most common species makes up 30% of its individuals (12 of 40), whereas species 1 makes up 62.5% of Woodland B's individuals (25 of 40), so most of Woodland B's beetles belong to one species [1].

Woodland A's D value is higher, 5.38 against 2.33, so Woodland A has greater biodiversity, because D combines richness and evenness [1].

(c) 1. A conifer plantation is usually planted with one or a few tree species under a uniform canopy. This probably gives beetles fewer kinds of food and shelter, so fewer species can find a niche [1].

2. Dense conifer shade probably reduces ground vegetation and gives a less varied leaf litter, removing the feeding and hiding sites that many beetle species use [1].

(d) Pitfall traps catch only beetles that move about on the ground, so species that live mainly in the canopy or fly are missed, and the species counts for each woodland may be incomplete [1].

(e) After felling, the plantation would regenerate by secondary succession, because soil remains after the disturbance [1]. Over 50 years, grasses and herbs, then shrubs and young trees, would colonise the site; as the canopy closes, shade, leaf litter and habitat variety would increase, so the beetle community would probably shift from species of open ground towards woodland species [1].

The [1] tags are illustrative mark points, not the official markscheme; any mark is provisional until your teacher or the IB awards it.

maa-t15.subject: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
maa-t15.question: I'm taking Mathematics: analysis and approaches SL (the course first assessed in 2021; my exams are in May 2027). Paper 1 (no calculator) Section A practice. Question 1 [6 marks]: Let f(x) = x² − 6x + k, where k is a constant. (a) Find the set of values of k for which the equation f(x) = 0 has two distinct real roots. [3] (b) For k = 5, write f(x) in the form (x − h)² + c, and state the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of y = f(x). [3] Question 2 [6 marks]: Let g(x) = 2x + 3 and h(x) = (x − 1)/2. (a) Find (h ∘ g)(x). [2] (b) Find g⁻¹(x). [2] (c) Solve the equation (h ∘ g)(x) = g⁻¹(x). [2] Question 3 [7 marks]: A bag contains 5 red counters and 3 blue counters. Two counters are taken at random, without replacement. (a) Find the probability that both counters are red. [2] (b) Find the probability that the two counters are of different colours. [2] (c) Given that at least one of the counters is blue, find the probability that both are blue. [3] Show full working.
maa-t15.response_text:
Assumption: SL, Paper 1 (no calculator), so every value is exact.

Question 1 [6 marks]

(a) Two distinct real roots need Δ > 0, where Δ = b² − 4ac with a = 1, b = −6, c = k:  M1
Δ = (−6)² − 4(1)(k)
36 − 4k > 0  A1
4k < 36
k < 9  A1

So the required values are k < 9.

(b) For k = 5, f(x) = x² − 6x + 5.
Complete the square on x² − 6x:  M1
x² − 6x = (x − 3)² − 9
f(x) = (x − 3)² − 9 + 5
f(x) = (x − 3)² − 4  A1
Check: (x − 3)² − 4 = x² − 6x + 9 − 4 = x² − 6x + 5.
Vertex: (3, −4)  A1

Question 2 [6 marks]

(a) (h ∘ g)(x) = h(g(x)) = (g(x) − 1)/2  M1
= (2x + 3 − 1)/2
= (2x + 2)/2
(h ∘ g)(x) = x + 1  A1
Check: at x = 0, g(0) = 3 and h(3) = 1 = 0 + 1.

(b) Let y = 2x + 3. Then x = (y − 3)/2, so
g⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2  M1A1
Check: g((x − 3)/2) = 2 × (x − 3)/2 + 3 = x.

(c) x + 1 = (x − 3)/2  M1
2x + 2 = x − 3
x = −5  A1
Check: the left side is −5 + 1 = −4 and the right side is (−5 − 3)/2 = −4.

Question 3 [7 marks]

Write R for red and B for blue. The draws are without replacement, so the second draw is from 7 counters.

(a) P(both red) = (5/8) × (4/7)  M1
= 20/56
= 5/14  A1
Check: C(5, 2)/C(8, 2) = 10/28 = 5/14.

(b) P(different colours) = P(RB) + P(BR)  M1
= (5/8)(3/7) + (3/8)(5/7)
= 15/56 + 15/56
= 30/56 = 15/28  A1
Check: 1 − P(RR) − P(BB) = 1 − 5/14 − 3/28 = 15/28.

(c) Let E be "at least one blue" and F be "both blue". Since F is contained in E, P(F ∩ E) = P(F).
P(E) = 1 − P(RR) = 1 − 5/14 = 9/14  M1
P(F) = (3/8)(2/7) = 3/28
P(F | E) = (3/28)/(9/14)  M1
= (3/28) × (14/9)
= 42/252
P(F | E) = 1/6  A1
Check by counting: selections with at least one blue number C(8, 2) − C(5, 2) = 28 − 10 = 18, of which C(3, 2) = 3 are both blue, so 3/18 = 1/6.

mai-t15.subject: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
mai-t15.question: I'm taking Mathematics: applications and interpretation SL (the course first assessed in 2021; my exams are in May 2027). Paper 1 practice question [13 marks]: Three wells supply water to the farms in a valley. On a map with coordinates in kilometres, the wells are at A(2, 1), B(8, 3) and C(4, 9). Each farm takes water from its nearest well. (a) Find the coordinates of the midpoint of AB. [2] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of AB, giving your answer in the form y = mx + c. [3] (c) The perpendicular bisector of BC has equation y = (2/3)x + 2. Find the coordinates of the point where the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC meet. [2] (d) Find the distance from this point to well A. [2] (e) A new farmhouse is built at P(5, 5). Determine which well it should take water from, justifying your answer. [3] (f) State what the point found in (c) represents in the Voronoi diagram of the three wells. [1] Show your working.
mai-t15.response_text:
Assumption: distances are straight-line distances on the map, in km.

(a) Midpoint of AB $= \left(\frac{2 + 8}{2},\ \frac{1 + 3}{2}\right)$ M1

$= (5,\ 2)$ (km) A1

(b) Gradient of AB $= \frac{3 - 1}{8 - 2} = \frac{1}{3}$

The perpendicular gradient $m$ satisfies $\frac{1}{3}m = -1$, so $m = -3$ M1

The line through $(5,\ 2)$ with gradient $-3$ is $y - 2 = -3(x - 5)$ M1

$y = -3x + 17$ A1

Check: $(6,\ -1)$ lies on this line, and $(6 - 2)^2 + (-1 - 1)^2 = 20 = (6 - 8)^2 + (-1 - 3)^2$.

(c) Equate the two line equations: $-3x + 17 = \frac{2}{3}x + 2$. Multiplying by 3 gives $-9x + 51 = 2x + 6$, so $11x = 45$. M1

$x = \frac{45}{11} = 4.0909\ldots$

$y = -3\left(\frac{45}{11}\right) + 17 = \frac{52}{11} = 4.7272\ldots$

The point is $(4.09,\ 4.73)$ (km). A1

Check: $\frac{2}{3}\left(\frac{45}{11}\right) + 2 = \frac{30}{11} + \frac{22}{11} = \frac{52}{11}$.

(d) $d = \sqrt{\left(\frac{45}{11} - 2\right)^2 + \left(\frac{52}{11} - 1\right)^2}$ M1

$= \sqrt{\left(\frac{23}{11}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{41}{11}\right)^2} = \frac{\sqrt{2210}}{11} = 4.2737\ldots$

The distance is $4.27$ km. A1

Check: the distances from the point to B and to C are also $\frac{\sqrt{2210}}{11}$, as they must be.

(e) Distance to A $= \sqrt{(5 - 2)^2 + (5 - 1)^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ km M1

Distance to B $= \sqrt{(5 - 8)^2 + (5 - 3)^2} = \sqrt{13} = 3.61$ km

Distance to C $= \sqrt{(5 - 4)^2 + (5 - 9)^2} = \sqrt{17} = 4.12$ km A1

The farmhouse is closest to well B (3.61 km, compared with 4.12 km and 5 km), so it should take its water from well B. R1

(f) The point in (c) is a Voronoi vertex: it is equidistant (4.27 km) from A, B and C, and it is the point where the boundaries of the three wells' cells meet. A1

cs-t15.subject: Computer Science
cs-t15.question: Computer Science, exams in May 2027 (the course first assessed in May 2027). Paper 1 Section A practice question on networks. A school's media department uploads video files from its local area network (LAN) to a cloud server over the school's internet connection. (a) Outline the role of a switch and of a router in this network. [2] (b) A video file is 1.8 GB and the school's upload speed is 40 Mbit/s. Calculate the minimum time, in minutes, needed to upload the file. Take 1 GB = 1000 MB and 1 byte = 8 bits. [3] (c) Files are sent in packets that each carry 1500 bytes of data. Calculate the number of packets needed to send a 6.0 MB file, taking 1 MB = 10⁶ bytes. [2] (d) Explain why the upload uses TCP rather than UDP. [3] (e) Describe how the file passes through the four layers of the TCP/IP model on its way from the school's computer to the cloud server. [4] (f) Compare static and dynamic routing for the school's connection to its cloud provider. [4] Show your working.
cs-t15.response_text:
Assumptions: this is treated as HL, because parts (e) and (f) cover HL-only content; 1 MB = 10⁶ bytes and 1 Mbit = 10⁶ bits, following the question's convention.

(a) [2]
Switch: forwards frames between the devices on the school's local area network, using MAC addresses, so local traffic goes only to the device it is addressed to.
Router: forwards packets between the local network and other networks, such as the school's internet connection to the cloud provider, using IP addresses.

(b) [3]
Working:
1.8 GB × 1000 MB per GB = 1800 MB
1800 MB × 10⁶ bytes per MB = 1.8 × 10⁹ bytes
1.8 × 10⁹ bytes × 8 bits per byte = 1.44 × 10¹⁰ bits
Upload speed 40 Mbit/s = 40 × 10⁶ bits per second = 4.0 × 10⁷ bits per second
Time = 1.44 × 10¹⁰ bits ÷ 4.0 × 10⁷ bits per second = 360 s
360 s ÷ 60 = 6.0 minutes
Answer: 6.0 minutes. This is the minimum, because packet headers, acknowledgements and any retransmissions add data and slow the real upload.

(c) [2]
Working:
6.0 MB × 10⁶ bytes per MB = 6 000 000 bytes
6 000 000 bytes ÷ 1500 bytes per packet = 4000 packets
Answer: 4000 packets. The division is exact, so no extra packet is needed.

(d) [3]
TCP is connection-oriented and reliable. Each segment is numbered and acknowledged, and any segment that is not acknowledged is sent again, so the server receives every part of the file. TCP also uses the sequence numbers to reassemble segments in their original order. UDP sends datagrams with no acknowledgement, no retransmission and no ordering, so packets lost on the connection would leave gaps in the video, and packets arriving out of order would scramble it. A slower upload is acceptable, but a damaged file is not, so TCP's extra overhead is worth paying.

(e) [4]
The file travels down the four layers on the school's computer, then up the four layers at the cloud server.
1. Application layer: the upload program gives the file to an application protocol, such as HTTPS, which adds its own header and passes the data down.
2. Transport layer: TCP divides the file into segments, adds a header with source and destination port numbers and sequence numbers, and passes each segment down.
3. Internet layer: IP adds a header with the school computer's IP address and the cloud server's IP address, creating packets. Each router uses the destination IP address to forward the packet across the networks.
4. Network access layer: each packet is placed in a frame with the MAC address of the next device (the switch or router) and sent over the cable or wireless link. At each hop the frame is replaced with one addressed to the next device, while the IP addresses stay the same.
At the cloud server, each layer removes its header in reverse order, and TCP reassembles the segments into the file for the upload program.

(f) [4]
Compare asks for similarities only, so each point below is a similarity.
1. Both let the school's router choose the next hop for each packet bound for the cloud provider.
2. Both rely on a routing table, in which each entry matches a destination network to an outgoing route.
3. Both base the route on the destination IP address in each packet's header.
4. Both leave the end-to-end delivery to TCP, which resends any lost segment whichever route the packets take.

(a) [2]
Rainfall depth: 38 mm = 0.038 m (Storm 1); 36 mm = 0.036 m (Storm 2)
Catchment area: 24 km² = 24 × 10⁶ m² (1 km² = 1000 m × 1000 m = 10⁶ m²) = 2.4 × 10⁷ m²
Volume of rain = depth × area
Storm 1: 0.038 m × 2.4 × 10⁷ m² = 9.12 × 10⁵ m³ [1]
Storm 2: 0.036 m × 2.4 × 10⁷ m² = 8.64 × 10⁵ m³ [1]

(b) [2]
Percentage of rain that left as storm runoff = runoff volume ÷ rain volume × 100
Storm 1: 1.82 × 10⁵ m³ ÷ 9.12 × 10⁵ m³ × 100 = 19.956%, so 20.0% (3 s.f.) [1]
Storm 2: 4.10 × 10⁵ m³ ÷ 8.64 × 10⁵ m³ × 100 = 47.4537%, so 47.5% (3 s.f.) [1]
The share rose from 20.0% to 47.5%, a rise of 27.5 percentage points.

(c) [4]
Growth of the built-up area reduced the catchment's storage of water and sent more of it quickly into the brook, so the flow at the gauging station rose and arrived sooner.

Less rain is stored in the ground. Roofs, roads and car parks replace permeable ground, so less rain infiltrates and is held in the soil store [1].

More rain moves as surface flow. The share of rain leaving as storm runoff rose from 20.0% in Storm 1 to 47.5% in Storm 2 (part (b)), so a larger flow reached the channel over the surface [1].

Water arrives sooner. The Geography specialist reports a "lag time of 12 hours for Storm 1 and 4.5 hours for Storm 2". Drains and sewers move water off roofs and roads into the brook more quickly than soil would, and the Geography specialist notes that "Both storms had peak rainfall at 09:30, so the difference in timing comes from the catchment itself." [1]

Peak flow rises. The Geography specialist reports that "the peak discharge rose by 200%, from 5.4 m³ s⁻¹ in Storm 1 to 16.2 m³ s⁻¹ in Storm 2". The larger, faster surface flow reaches the channel together, so the peak rises [1].

A school's media department uploads video files from its local area network (LAN) to a cloud server over the school's internet connection. (a) Outline the role of a switch and of a router in this network. [2] (b) A video file is 1.8 GB and the school's upload speed is 40 Mbit/s. Calculate the minimum time, in minutes, needed to upload the file. Take 1 GB = 1000 MB and 1 byte = 8 bits. [3] (c) Files are sent in packets that each carry 1500 bytes of data. Calculate the number of packets needed to send a 6.0 MB file, taking 1 MB = 10⁶ bytes. [2] (d) Explain why the upload uses TCP rather than UDP. [3] (e) Describe how the file passes through the four layers of the TCP/IP model on its way from the school's computer to the cloud server. [4] (f) Compare static and dynamic routing for the school's connection to its cloud provider. [4] Show your working.
cs-t15-revised.response_text:
Assumptions: this is treated as HL, because parts (e) and (f) cover HL-only content. For part (b), the units used for each quantity are: 1 GB = 1000 MB and 1 byte = 8 bits, as the question states. The question does not define MB in bytes for part (b), so this answer uses 1 MB = 10⁶ bytes, the convention given in part (c). The question does not define Mbit for part (b) either, so this answer reads Mbit as 10⁶ bits, the SI meaning of the prefix M. The conversion from MB to bytes is the only step that depends on the MB reading; if your paper defines MB differently, change that one step.

(a) [2]
Switch: forwards frames between the devices on the school's local area network, using MAC addresses, so local traffic goes only to the device it is addressed to.
Router: forwards packets between the local network and other networks, such as the school's internet connection to the cloud provider, using IP addresses.

(b) [3]
Working (units shown for each quantity):
1.8 GB × 1000 MB per GB = 1800 MB
1800 MB × 10⁶ bytes per MB = 1.8 × 10⁹ bytes
1.8 × 10⁹ bytes × 8 bits per byte = 1.44 × 10¹⁰ bits
Upload speed: 40 Mbit/s = 40 × 10⁶ bits per second = 4.0 × 10⁷ bits per second
Time = 1.44 × 10¹⁰ bits ÷ 4.0 × 10⁷ bits per second = 360 s
360 s ÷ 60 s per minute = 6.0 minutes
Answer: 6.0 minutes. This is the minimum, because packet headers, acknowledgements and any retransmissions add data and slow the real upload.

(c) [2]
Working:
6.0 MB × 10⁶ bytes per MB = 6 000 000 bytes
6 000 000 bytes ÷ 1500 bytes per packet = 4000 packets
Answer: 4000 packets. The division is exact, so no extra packet is needed.

(d) [3]
TCP is connection-oriented and reliable. Each segment is numbered and acknowledged, and any segment that is not acknowledged is sent again, so the server receives every part of the file. TCP also uses the sequence numbers to reassemble segments in their original order. UDP sends datagrams with no acknowledgement, no retransmission and no ordering, so packets lost on the connection would leave gaps in the video, and packets arriving out of order would scramble it. A slower upload is acceptable, but a damaged file is not, so TCP's extra overhead is worth paying.

(e) [4]
The file travels down the four layers on the school's computer, then up the four layers at the cloud server.
1. Application layer: the upload program gives the file to an application protocol, such as HTTPS, which adds its own header and passes the data down.
2. Transport layer: TCP divides the file into segments, adds a header with source and destination port numbers and sequence numbers, and passes each segment down.
3. Internet layer: IP adds a header with the school computer's IP address and the cloud server's IP address, creating packets. Each router uses the destination IP address to forward the packet across the networks.
4. Network access layer: each packet is placed in a frame with the MAC address of the next device (the switch or router) and sent over the cable or wireless link. At each hop the frame is replaced with one addressed to the next device, while the IP addresses stay the same.
At the cloud server, each layer removes its header in reverse order, and TCP reassembles the segments into the file for the upload program.

(f) [4]
Compare asks for similarities only, so each point below is a similarity.
1. Both let the school's router choose the next hop for each packet bound for the cloud provider.
2. Both rely on a routing table, in which each entry matches a destination network to an outgoing route.
3. Both base the route on the destination IP address in each packet's header.
4. Both leave the end-to-end delivery to TCP, which resends any lost segment whichever route the packets take.
Teaching note: if your paper asks you to contrast them, add the differences. Static routes are entered by an administrator and do not adapt to failures, whereas dynamic routes are updated automatically by routing protocols.

v = √(9.016 m² s⁻²) = 3.0027 m s⁻¹, so v = 3.00 m s⁻¹ (3 s.f.)

(b) [2]
Principle: momentum is conserved, since no external horizontal force acts during the collision.
Symbols: m₁ = 1.2 × 10⁴ kg and u₁ = 3.0 m s⁻¹ (the moving wagon, before the collision); m₂ = 8.0 × 10³ kg and u₂ = 0 m s⁻¹ (the stationary wagon); v = common velocity of the coupled wagons just after the collision.
m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v
(1.2 × 10⁴ kg)(3.0 m s⁻¹) + (8.0 × 10³ kg)(0 m s⁻¹) = (1.2 × 10⁴ kg + 8.0 × 10³ kg)v
3.6 × 10⁴ kg m s⁻¹ = (2.0 × 10⁴ kg)v
v = 1.8 m s⁻¹, in the original direction of motion

(c) [3]
Before: E_k = ½m₁u₁² = ½(1.2 × 10⁴ kg)(3.0 m s⁻¹)² = 5.4 × 10⁴ J
After: E_k = ½(m₁ + m₂)v² = ½(2.0 × 10⁴ kg)(1.8 m s⁻¹)² = 3.24 × 10⁴ J
Transferred to other forms: ΔE = 5.4 × 10⁴ J − 3.24 × 10⁴ J = 2.16 × 10⁴ J, so ΔE = 2.2 × 10⁴ J (2 s.f.)
As a percentage: (2.16 × 10⁴ J / 5.4 × 10⁴ J) × 100% = 40%

(d) [2]
Principle: impulse equals change in momentum, FΔt = Δp. The direction of motion is taken as positive, and the buffer force F is assumed to be the only horizontal force on the wagons (level track, friction and air resistance ignored).
Values: m = 2.0 × 10⁴ kg (the coupled wagons); u = +1.8 m s⁻¹ (their velocity just after the collision, from (b)); v_f = 0 m s⁻¹ (at rest); Δt = 0.60 s.
Δp = m(v_f − u) = (2.0 × 10⁴ kg)(0 m s⁻¹ − 1.8 m s⁻¹) = −3.6 × 10⁴ kg m s⁻¹
F = Δp / Δt = (−3.6 × 10⁴ kg m s⁻¹) / (0.60 s) = −6.0 × 10⁴ N
The average force is 6.0 × 10⁴ N, opposite to the direction of motion.

(e) [2]
Principle: ½kx² = E_k, with E_k = 3.24 × 10⁴ J from (c).
x² = (2 × 3.24 × 10⁴ J) / (2.0 × 10⁶ N m⁻¹) = 3.24 × 10⁻² m²
x = 0.18 m = 18 cm (2 s.f.)

(f) [2]
Momentum: the forces between the wagons during coupling are an equal and opposite pair (Newton's third law), so they are internal to the system. The weights are balanced by normal forces and friction is ignored, so there is no external horizontal force and the total momentum is conserved.
Kinetic energy: the wagons stick together in an inelastic collision. Part of the kinetic energy becomes internal energy in the couplings (deformation and heating) and sound, so the kinetic energy after the collision is less, while the total energy is still conserved.

maa-t15-revised.subject: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
maa-t15-revised.question: I'm taking Mathematics: analysis and approaches SL (the course first assessed in 2021; my exams are in May 2027). Paper 1 (no calculator) Section A practice. Question 1 [6 marks]: Let f(x) = x² − 6x + k, where k is a constant. (a) Find the set of values of k for which the equation f(x) = 0 has two distinct real roots. [3] (b) For k = 5, write f(x) in the form (x − h)² + c, and state the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of y = f(x). [3] Question 2 [6 marks]: Let g(x) = 2x + 3 and h(x) = (x − 1)/2. (a) Find (h ∘ g)(x). [2] (b) Find g⁻¹(x). [2] (c) Solve the equation (h ∘ g)(x) = g⁻¹(x). [2] Question 3 [7 marks]: A bag contains 5 red counters and 3 blue counters. Two counters are taken at random, without replacement. (a) Find the probability that both counters are red. [2] (b) Find the probability that the two counters are of different colours. [2] (c) Given that at least one of the counters is blue, find the probability that both are blue. [3] Show full working.
maa-t15-revised.response_text:
Assumption: SL, Paper 1 (no calculator), so every value is exact.

Question 1 [6 marks]

(a) Two distinct real roots need Δ > 0, where Δ = b² − 4ac with a = 1, b = −6, c = k:  M1
Δ = (−6)² − 4(1)(k)
Δ = 36 − 4k
36 − 4k > 0  A1
−4k > −36 (subtract 36 from both sides)
k < 9 (divide both sides by −4, reversing the inequality)  A1

So the required values are k < 9.

(b) For k = 5, f(x) = x² − 6x + 5.
Complete the square on x² − 6x:  M1
x² − 6x = (x − 3)² − 9
f(x) = (x − 3)² − 9 + 5
f(x) = (x − 3)² − 4  A1
Check: (x − 3)² − 4 = x² − 6x + 9 − 4 = x² − 6x + 5.
Vertex: (3, −4)  A1

Question 2 [6 marks]

(a) (h ∘ g)(x) = h(g(x)) = (g(x) − 1)/2  M1
= (2x + 3 − 1)/2
= (2x + 2)/2
(h ∘ g)(x) = x + 1  A1
Check: at x = 0, g(0) = 3 and h(3) = 1 = 0 + 1.

(b) Let y = 2x + 3. Then x = (y − 3)/2, so
g⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2  M1A1
Check: g((x − 3)/2) = 2 × (x − 3)/2 + 3 = x.

(c) x + 1 = (x − 3)/2  M1
2x + 2 = x − 3
x = −5  A1
Check: the left side is −5 + 1 = −4 and the right side is (−5 − 3)/2 = −4.

Question 3 [7 marks]

Write R for red and B for blue. The draws are without replacement, so the second draw is from 7 counters.

(a) P(both red) = (5/8) × (4/7)  M1
= 20/56
= 5/14  A1
Check: C(5, 2)/C(8, 2) = 10/28 = 5/14.

(b) P(different colours) = P(RB) + P(BR)  M1
= (5/8)(3/7) + (3/8)(5/7)
= 15/56 + 15/56
= 30/56 = 15/28  A1
Check: 1 − P(RR) − P(BB) = 1 − 5/14 − 3/28 = 15/28.

(c) Let E be "at least one blue" and F be "both blue". Since F is contained in E, P(F ∩ E) = P(F).
P(E) = 1 − P(RR) = 1 − 5/14 = 9/14  M1
P(F) = (3/8)(2/7) = 3/28
P(F | E) = (3/28)/(9/14)  M1
= (3/28) × (14/9)
= 42/252
P(F | E) = 1/6  A1
Check by counting: selections with at least one blue number C(8, 2) − C(5, 2) = 28 − 10 = 18, of which C(3, 2) = 3 are both blue, so 3/18 = 1/6.

ch-p9b-revised.subject: Chemistry
ch-p9b-revised.question: I'm a Chemistry SL student (the course first assessed in 2025; my exams are in May 2027). Paper 1B-style practice on preparing solutions. A Biology student will use your concentrations in an osmosis practical with potato tissue, so give the concentration of the stock solution and of each diluted solution clearly, in mol dm⁻³, to three significant figures. A technician dissolved 84.20 g of sucrose, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, in distilled water and made the solution up to 250.0 cm³ in a volumetric flask. Use the relative atomic masses C 12.01, H 1.01 and O 16.00. (a) Calculate the molar mass of sucrose. [1] (b) Calculate the concentration of the stock solution. [2] (c) Four diluted solutions were made by pipetting 10.00 cm³, 20.00 cm³, 30.00 cm³ and 40.00 cm³ of the stock solution into separate 50.00 cm³ volumetric flasks and making each up to the mark with distilled water. Calculate the concentration of each diluted solution. [2] (d) The balance reads to ±0.01 g and the 250.0 cm³ flask has an uncertainty of ±0.30 cm³. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the concentration of the stock solution, ignoring all other uncertainties. [2] (e) Calculate the number of sucrose molecules in 1.00 cm³ of the most dilute solution. [2] (f) Explain why a volumetric flask, rather than a measuring cylinder, is used to make up the solutions. [1] Show your working with units.
ch-p9b-revised.response_text:
Constants and data used: M(C) = 12.01, M(H) = 1.01, M(O) = 16.00 (from the question). Avogadro constant N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ (standard value). I assume the sucrose dissolved completely before the flask was made up to the mark.

(a) Molar mass of sucrose [1]

M(C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁) = 12(12.01) + 22(1.01) + 11(16.00) = 144.12 + 22.22 + 176.00 = 342.34 g mol⁻¹ [1]

(b) Concentration of the stock solution [2]

n(sucrose) = m ÷ M = 84.20 g ÷ 342.34 g mol⁻¹ = 0.245954 mol (unrounded) [1]
V = 250.0 cm³ ÷ 1000 (since 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³) = 0.2500 dm³
c(stock) = n ÷ V = 0.245954 mol ÷ 0.2500 dm³ = 0.98382 mol dm⁻³, so c(stock) = 0.984 mol dm⁻³ (3 s.f.) [1]

(c) Concentration of each diluted solution [2]

Each diluted solution is made up to 50.00 cm³, so c(diluted) = c(stock) × V(pipetted) ÷ 50.00 cm³. The unrounded stock concentration (0.98382 mol dm⁻³) is used. [1]
10.00 cm³: 0.98382 × (10.00 ÷ 50.00) = 0.19676 mol dm⁻³, so 0.197 mol dm⁻³ [1 for the values]
20.00 cm³: 0.98382 × (20.00 ÷ 50.00) = 0.39353 mol dm⁻³, so 0.394 mol dm⁻³
30.00 cm³: 0.98382 × (30.00 ÷ 50.00) = 0.59029 mol dm⁻³, so 0.590 mol dm⁻³
40.00 cm³: 0.98382 × (40.00 ÷ 50.00) = 0.78706 mol dm⁻³, so 0.787 mol dm⁻³

(d) Percentage uncertainty in the stock concentration [2]

Only the balance and flask uncertainties are used, as the question specifies.
Mass: 0.01 g ÷ 84.20 g × 100 = 0.0119% [1]
Volume: 0.30 cm³ ÷ 250.0 cm³ × 100 = 0.120%
For a quotient, the percentage uncertainties add: 0.0119% + 0.120% = 0.132%, so the percentage uncertainty is 0.13%. [1]

(e) Sucrose molecules in 1.00 cm³ of the most dilute solution [2]

The most dilute solution is the 10.00 cm³ dilution, with c = 0.19676 mol dm⁻³ (unrounded).
V = 1.00 cm³ ÷ 1000 (since 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³) = 1.00 × 10⁻³ dm³
n = c × V = 0.19676 mol dm⁻³ × 1.00 × 10⁻³ dm³ = 1.9676 × 10⁻⁴ mol [1]
N = n × N_A = 1.9676 × 10⁻⁴ mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 1.18 × 10²⁰ molecules (3 s.f.) [1]
Using the rounded 0.197 mol dm⁻³ would give 1.19 × 10²⁰, so the unrounded value is carried.

(f) Why a volumetric flask is used [1]

A volumetric flask has a single calibrated mark and is designed to contain one precisely known volume, for example 250.0 cm³ ± 0.30 cm³ as in part (d). A measuring cylinder is less precise, so the volume of each solution, and therefore its concentration, would be less certain. [1]

Concentrations for the Biology student, in mol dm⁻³ (3 s.f.):
Stock solution: 0.984
Made from 10.00 cm³ of stock: 0.197
Made from 20.00 cm³ of stock: 0.394
Made from 30.00 cm³ of stock: 0.590
Made from 40.00 cm³ of stock: 0.787

If you want more practice, try part (e) for the 40.00 cm³ dilution.
